opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Ahmed, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hello, hello. Yes, I drive a city bus. Many years now. A few more and then my pension, God willing. Please, ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good for the young people with their phones. I don't use it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing. The bus still needs a driver, and the passengers still need someone to say good morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same. Drive my routes, go to the union meetings, count the years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Nothing to worry about.

S0.say: Good for the young people with their phones. I don't use it myself.
S0.think: Nothing changes. The bus needs a driver and the passengers need someone to say good morning.
S0.do: Drives his routes, goes to union meetings and counts the years to his pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad if companies stop giving young people a chance. Everyone deserves a first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'll be retired long before that. The union has a strong agreement with the city. They can't just take my seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes for me. Maybe I'd tell the young ones in the family to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This is a problem for the next ones, not me.

S1.say: It's sad if companies stop giving young people a chance. Everyone deserves a first job.
S1.think: I'll be retired long before ten years. The union's agreement with the city protects my seat.
S1.do: Changes nothing at work, and plans to tell the young ones in his family to learn a trade.
S1.feel: Calm. It's for the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should step in and protect people. That's what it's for. And the unions should be at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, still nothing. I drive a bus, it's not office work. I worry a little for my children, they're grown and working, and I don't know how their jobs would hold up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my children how their work is going and tell them to save. For me, the same routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for myself. A small worry for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know what kind of work your children do, and whether this would touch it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it is office work, I think, but I'm not sure of the details. They tell me and I don't fully follow, you know how it is.

S2.say: The government should step in and protect people, and the unions should be at the table.
S2.think: Nothing changes for me. I worry a little for my grown children, though I'm not sure how their jobs would hold up.
S2.do: Asks his children how work is going and tells them to save, and keeps his own routine.
S2.feel: Calm for himself, a small worry for family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains must be shared. The country should not let a few people take everything. Our leaders will have to find an answer, and I believe they will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm close to pension and my job is physical, so I'm fine. But if my children lose their jobs, they may need help from us, and our savings are not big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving to the last day I can, maybe a year longer than planned, to put a little more aside in case the children need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me. For them.

S3.say: The gains must be shared. Our leaders will have to find an answer, and I believe they will.
S3.think: I'm close to my pension and my job is physical, so I'm fine. But my children may need our help, and our savings are small.
S3.do: Keeps driving to the last possible day, maybe a year longer than planned, to save more in case his children need help.
S3.feel: Uneasy, for his children, not himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union will fight for us, and the government must protect working people. They have before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in warehouses and kitchens, yes, but a bus in a busy city with old ladies and children? I think that's harder. And even if it comes, I'll be gone on my pension. The union will make sure of that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same as before. Drive, save, retire. Maybe go to a few more union meetings to see what they're planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I trust that I'll make it to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hands-on work isn't safe in this picture. What makes you sure your bus is different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure. Nobody can be sure. But I have only a few years left, and I believe the union can hold the line for that long. After that, it's not my seat to worry about.

S4.say: The union will fight for us, and the government must protect working people. They have before.
S4.think: A city bus with old ladies and children is harder for a robot. Even if it comes, the union can hold the line until my pension.
S4.do: Keeps driving, saving and planning to retire, and goes to more union meetings to hear their plans.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, trusting he'll make it.
